n:
- *Paul, an apostle*: Apostles were representatives with authority given by a church or council (for example, {{2 Corinthians 8:23|2 Corinthians 8:23}}; {{Philippians 2:25|Philippians 2:25}}). However, the Jerusalem church did not appoint Paul as an apostle. Instead, Jesus Christ himself chose Paul, giving him Christ’s authority ({{Acts 9:1-15|Acts 9:1–15}}; {{Acts 26:12-20|26:12}}{{Acts 9:1-15|–}}{{Acts 26:12-20|20}}; see also {{Romans 1:5|Romans 1:5}}). This authority was equal to that of other apostles. 

- Paul said that God the Father gave him his authority as an apostle. This happened because God raised Jesus from the dead. The fact that Jesus rose from death made it possible for Paul to receive his special work from God.

In all his letters, Paul introduces himself and greets the recipients. This greeting stands out because: 

- Paul strongly asserts his authority as an apostle ({{Galatians 1:1|1:1}}). 

- Instead of offering thanks, prayer, or praise, he gives a rebuke ({{Galatians 1:6-10|1:6}}{{Acts 9:1-15|–}}{{Galatians 1:6-10|10}}).

Paul was very concerned about the believers in Galatia. They had believed the good news Paul taught them about Jesus.

But then after Paul left other teachers went to Galatia. They taught things that went against the good news about Jesus. The Galatians started to believe those teachings.

God had sent Paul to preach the good news. That was Paul’s work as an apostle.

Paul was completely sure about the truth of the message that he preached. He preached that Jesus gave his life for the sins of human beings. Jesus sets those who believe in him free from this evil world.

That was how Paul described the power of sin, death and evil. God the Father wanted Jesus to set people free. All teaching about Jesus must agree with this. If it doesn’t, followers of Jesus must refuse to believe it.

Some people were against Paul and questioned whether he was a true apostle. They did not believe he was honest and did not think he had the right to be a leader in the church. So Paul begins his letter by explaining that he really was an apostle with authority from God.

- *all the brothers with me*: Paul likely wrote from Antioch of Syria. Antioch was the center of Paul’s ministry and the first hub of Gentile Christianity (see {{Acts 11:20-26|Acts 11:20–26}}). Paul was not alone, although his opponents in Galatia might have suggested that, but he was in fellowship with an important New Testament church. 

- Paul probably founded the churches of Galatia during his first missionary journey ({{Acts 13:4-14:26|Acts 13:4–14:26}}; see Galatians Book Introduction, “Recipients”).

*Grace and peace to you from God*: This is a common greeting by Paul (see also study note on 1 Corinthians 1:3). It combines Greek and Hebrew greetings. "Grace" (Greek *charis*) is similar to "greetings" (Greek *chairein*). "Peace" reflects Hebrew *shalom*. Paul included both Jewish and non-Jewish Christians (compare {{Galatians 3:28|Galatians 3:28}}). The Galatians risked losing God's grace and peace ({{Galatians 3:1-4|3:1–4}}; {{Galatians 5:1-4|5:1}}{{Galatians 3:1-4|–}}{{Galatians 5:1-4|4}}).
Paul followed the common style for first-century letters. He included a greeting, wished for well-being, and introduced the main topic, the good news about Jesus.

- Since Jesus fully rescued us from our sins, we do not need to try to save ourselves. 

- Christian faith rescues us from the evil world we live in (see {{Galatians 4:8-12|4:8}}{{Galatians 3:1-4|–}}{{Galatians 4:8-12|12}}; {{Galatians 5:13-26|5:13}}{{Galatians 3:1-4|–}}{{Galatians 5:13-26|26}}).

This summary of the good news about Jesus is the basis for the following criticism ({{Galatians 1:6-10|1:6}}{{Galatians 3:1-4|–}}{{Galatians 1:6-10|10}}). It might be a creed or statement of faith that Paul used to remind the Galatians of the message they had accepted before.
We should thank God alone for salvation because it is his work alone.

- The Galatians were *deserting* (or abandoning) God by rejecting the good news about Jesus that Paul shared. Instead, they were depending on the law. God called them to himself through Christ's loving mercy, not through the law ({{Galatians 2:16|2:16}}). 

- *the One who called you*: See {{Galatians 1:15|1:15}}; {{Romans 8:30|Romans 8:30}}; {{Romans 9:24|9:24}}; {{Romans 11:29|11:29}}. 

- *a different gospel*: Some people taught that non-Jewish Christians had to be circumcised to join God's family. Paul rejected any requirement other than faith in Jesus (see {{Galatians 5:2-4|Galatians 5:2–4}}).

*I am amazed*: In most of his letters, Paul usually expressed gratitude and prayed for those who received his letters after his greeting (for example, {{Romans 1:8-10|Romans 1:8–10}}; {{1 Corinthians 1:4-5|1 Corinthians 1:4}}{{Romans 1:8-10|–}}{{1 Corinthians 1:4-5|5}}; {{Philippians 1:3-6|Philippians 1:3}}{{Romans 1:8-10|–}}{{Philippians 1:3-6|6}}; {{Colossians 1:3-5|Colossians 1:3}}{{Romans 1:8-10|–}}{{Colossians 1:3-5|5}}; {{2 Thessalonians 1:3-12|2 Thessalonians 1:3}}{{Romans 1:8-10|–}}{{2 Thessalonians 1:3-12|12}}). But he had nothing positive to say about the Galatian church.

- The "different gospel" ({{Galatians 1:6|1:6}}) was a distortion and not the true message of salvation. The only way to be saved is through faith in Christ. Adding any extra requirements changes the message and it is no longer the good news. 

- *some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ*: The Judaizers (a group insisting on Jewish customs) knew they were altering the good news about Jesus to match their beliefs.

- *let him be under a curse!* (literally *Let that person be anathema*): The Greek word *anathema* often translates the Hebrew *kherem*, which in the Old Testament means something dedicated to God for complete destruction (see {{Leviticus 27:28-29|Leviticus 27:28–29}}; compare {{Romans 9:3|Romans 9:3}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:3|1 Corinthians 12:3}}; {{1 Corinthians 16:22|16:22}}). Paul called for God's strongest wrath on those who distort the good news about Jesus ({{Galatians 1:7|Galatians 1:7}}). 

- *even if we or an angel from heaven*: No one is allowed to change the good news (compare {{Galatians 2:6-10|2:6–10}}, {{Galatians 2:11-14|11–14}}).

*a gospel contrary to the one you received*: the gospel (the good news about Jesus) the Galatians had received was exactly what Paul had preached to them ({{Galatians 1:8|1:8}}; compare {{2 Thessalonians 2:15|2 Thessalonians 2:15}}).

- The tone and content of this letter show that Paul did not seek to win people's approval. The Judaizers likely criticized Paul for trying to please people by focusing only on faith and grace, not including the law, which they saw as the whole message. 

- Being Christ’s servant means staying true to Christ, no matter how others react (see {{Acts 5:29|Acts 5:29}}; {{Ephesians 6:5-6|Ephesians 6:5–6}}; {{1 Thessalonians 2:3-6|1 Thessalonians 2:3–6}}).

*the gospel I preached*: Paul taught that people are made right with God by grace and through faith, not by following the law (see {{Galatians 2:16-17|2:16–17}}; {{Romans 10:9-13|Romans 10:9–13}}; {{Ephesians 2:8-9|Ephesians 2:8–9}}).

Paul explained how he learnt the good news about Jesus. At first Paul hadn’t believed that Jesus was the Messiah.

Paul had always been a very faithful Jew. He knew Jewish laws and teachings better than most other Jews did. He was a Pharisee. He used to put Jesus’ followers in prison for not obeying Jewish laws.

Then Jesus appeared to him. Jesus showed Paul that he was the Son of God. This completely changed Paul’s life. This story is told in Acts chapter 9.

After that, Paul spent his life sharing the good news about Jesus. He met other apostles like Peter and James. Together with other believers in Judea, they were happy that Paul was following Jesus.

The Judaizers (people who insisted on following Jewish customs) came to Galatia. They preached that both faith and circumcision were necessary. They questioned Paul's authority as an apostle and tried to discredit his message. Paul defended his authority by showing that past events proved his message was the true good news.

- *I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it*: Jewish scholars mainly relied on teachers. The Judaizers claimed Paul received his special mission and message from the other apostles, but then had unfaithfully changed the message. 

- *I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ*: See {{Galatians 1:17|1:17}}; {{Acts 9:3-15|Acts 9:3–15}}; {{Acts 26:12-18|26:12–18}}. Paul's unique experience gave him special authority and insight. However, he learned many things about the life of Jesus from other people (for example, {{Galatians 1:18|Galatians 1:18}}; {{1 Corinthians 11:23-26|1 Corinthians 11:23–26}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:3-11|15:3–11}}).

To show that his message was not from human reasoning (*devised by man*, {{Galatians 1:11|1:11}}), Paul explains his life before meeting Jesus. He was a very successful Jew (see {{Acts 8:1-3|Acts 8:1–3}}; {{Acts 22:1-5|22:1}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Acts 22:1-5|5}}; {{Acts 26:4-5|26:4}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Acts 26:4-5|5}}; {{Philippians 3:4-7|Philippians 3:4}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Philippians 3:4-7|7}}). His opposition to God's church and strict following of Judaism showed his belief in the law before Christ confronted him ({{Galatians 1:15-16|Galatians 1:15}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Galatians 1:15-16|16}}).

*zealous for the traditions of my fathers:* Paul was very passionate about following the Jewish religious traditions he learned from his ancestors (see {{Mark 7:6-13|Mark 7:6}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Mark 7:6-13|13}}).

- *God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb: *God chose Paul for special work even before he was born. This is like how God chose other leaders (see {{Jeremiah 1:5|Jeremiah 1:5}}; {{Psalm 139:13-16|Psalm 139:13}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Psalm 139:13-16|16}}; {{Isaiah 49:1-6|Isaiah 49:1}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Isaiah 49:1-6|6}}; {{Romans 9:10-13|Romans 9:10}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Romans 9:10-13|13}}). 

- *called me by His grace:* For Paul's conversion story (how he became a follower of Jesus), see {{Acts 9:1-19|Acts 9:1}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Acts 9:1-19|19}}; {{Acts 22:1-21|22:1}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Acts 22:1-21|21}}; {{Acts 26:9-23|26:9}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Acts 26:9-23|23}}. 

- Paul was called to share the good news about Jesus with non-Jews ({{Galatians 2:7|Galatians 2:7}}). He even taught other apostles what this meant (see {{Galatians 2:11-21|Galatians 2:11}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Galatians 2:11-21|21}}). 

- *to reveal His Son in me*: This might refer to Paul's meeting with Christ ({{Acts 9:1-19|Acts 9:1}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Acts 9:1-19|19}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 9:1|1 Corinthians 9:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:8|15:8}}). *In me* might also mean an inner revelation (see {{Galatians 2:20|Galatians 2:20}}; {{Galatians 4:6-7|4:6}}{{Acts 8:1-3|–}}{{Galatians 4:6-7|7}}) and suggests that Paul's changed heart showed Christ to others.

Paul learned directly from the Lord and did not consult with any person, not even the other apostles. Paul was independent from the other apostles but still agreed with them ({{Galatians 2:1-10|2:1–10}}).

- Paul considered his role as an apostle equal to that of the original disciples (see {{1 Corinthians 9:1|1 Corinthians 9:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:5-9|15:5–9}}; compare {{Acts 1:22|Acts 1:22}}; {{Acts 10:41|10:41}}). 

- Paul's journey to Arabia is not mentioned elsewhere. He likely developed his understanding of the good news about Jesus during that time. Paul was familiar with:

- the Scriptures (see {{Acts 22:3|Acts 22:3}}), 

- the beliefs of the first Christians (see {{Acts 8:1|Acts 8:1}}), and

- what others had shared with him since he became a follower of Jesus.

- *Only after three years *(or *in the third year*): This could be three years after Paul became a follower of Jesus or three years after his return from Arabia. This event is likely the visit mentioned in {{Acts 9:26-30|Acts 9:26–30}}. 

- *to confer with Cephas* (Peter): Peter had something Paul did not—personal experience with Jesus during his time on Earth. 

- Paul spent fifteen days with Peter. This was not enough time for Peter to become Paul's teacher, but it gave them enough time to talk carefully about what they were teaching people about Jesus.

Peter and James spent fifteen days discussing Paul's message, which matched theirs. Paul did not get his authority from the Jerusalem church. His role and authority as an apostle was independent of Jerusalem.
*I assure you before God*: Paul swears before God to emphasize that his story about his trip to Jerusalem is true.
Paul was not working under the guidance of the apostles in Jerusalem or the churches in Judea.

The church in Jerusalem was very happy when Paul became a follower of Jesus. This change (compare {{Galatians 1:13-14|1:13–14}}) and his message were both God's work (compare {{Acts 9:31|Acts 9:31}}). The way Paul taught about Jesus matched what the Jerusalem church believed.

- Counting fourteen years from Paul's conversion ({{Galatians 1:15-17|1:15–17}}), instead of from his previous visit ({{Galatians 1:18|1:18}}), fits well with the events in Acts. 

- The Galatian Christians knew who Barnabas was. This suggests that Paul and Barnabas first shared the good news about Jesus with them during their first missionary trip together ({{Acts 13:4-14:26|Acts 13:4–14:26}}; see Galatians Book Introduction, "Recipients"). 

- Titus was a non-Jewish believer who worked closely with Paul to help lead and strengthen churches. For more on Titus, see the "Titus" Profile.

Fourteen years after Paul started following Jesus as the Messiah, he went to Jerusalem. He met with James, Peter and John. They were three of Jesus’ most trusted disciples. They spread the message about Jesus among the Jewish people.

They listened to Paul and agreed with everything he preached. They understood that God had appointed Paul to preach to Gentiles. Paul explained this to the Galatians so that they would trust his teaching. It was another way to show that he hadn’t made up the good news about Jesus. He preached the same good news that other important church leaders preached.

Part of the good news is that Gentile believers don’t have to follow the Law of Moses. Gentile believers who are males don’t have to be circumcised. This was talked about in Acts chapter 15. Titus was an example of this.

When Paul visited Jerusalem for the second time, the other apostles agreed that what he was teaching was correct. According to tradition, Paul was writing about the important meeting of church leaders described in {{Acts 15:1-41|Acts 15:1–41}}. However, it is more likely that Paul was talking about his earlier visit to Jerusalem ({{Acts 11:30|Acts 11:30}}; {{Acts 12:25|12:25}}; see Galatians Book Introduction, "Date of Writing").

- If Paul's visit in {{Galatians 2:1-10|2:1–10}} was the same visit described in {{Acts 11:30|Acts 11:30}}, then God might have shown his will through the prophet Agabus's message and the church's decision to send help during a famine ({{Acts 11:27-29|Acts 11:27–29}}). 

- If Paul needed approval from Jerusalem's leaders, he would have met them openly. Their private meeting shows no one thought he needed public approval. 

- *to those recognized as leaders*: Paul does not speak about those leaders as if they were extremely important. He probably wrote this way because false teachers were giving these leaders too much respect and honor.

- Paul shared his message with the apostles in Jerusalem, not for approval, but to ensure agreement, preventing a split between Jewish and non-Jewish groups. 

- *for fear that I was running or had already run in vain*: A division between Jewish and non-Jewish Christians would harm the unity Christ established ({{Galatians 3:28|Galatians 3:28}}).

The apostles in Jerusalem fully agreed with Paul's message. They all believed the same good news: God's grace comes through faith in Christ, not by following the law. The Jerusalem apostles clearly did not believe that circumcision was necessary for a non-Jew like Titus.

- Paul called some supposed believers false, saying they were not Christians. They did not understand or truly accept the good news about Jesus, unlike the apostles in Jerusalem ({{Galatians 2:3|2:3}}). 

- *had come in under false pretenses*: Paul suggests that a larger group of Jewish "Christians" opposed his preaching (see {{Acts 15:5|Acts 15:5}}) and supported the false teachers who joined the church. 

- Requiring non-Jewish Christians to follow Jewish law would trap them in rules and deny the good news of Jesus (see {{Galatians 3:23-4:11|Galatians 3:23–4:11}}).
The false Christians entered the church in either Jerusalem or Antioch to weaken Paul's message. He taught that non-Jews (Gentiles) do not have to obey Jewish practices like circumcision.

- *We did not give in to them for a moment*: Titus was not circumcised ({{Galatians 2:3|2:3}}). Paul did not require circumcision for non-Jewish Christians. 

- *so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you*: The false teaching would ruin the the gospel (the good news about Jesus) by adding extra requirements and questioning the effectiveness of the death of Jesus and the grace of God (compare {{Galatians 2:11-21|2:11–21}}).

- The apostles in Jerusalem were seen as great leaders because they knew Jesus during his time on Earth. However, this did not give them more authority than Paul. What mattered most was Jesus personally choosing them (see {{1 Corinthians 9:1|1 Corinthians 9:1}}; compare {{2 Corinthians 12:11-12|2 Corinthians 12:11–12}}). 

- *God does not show favoritism*: The Judaizers (a group insisting on Jewish customs) likely thought the Jerusalem apostles' direct connection to Jesus was an advantage. Paul argues that favoritism is not in God's character (compare {{Leviticus 19:15-16|Leviticus 19:15–16}}; {{Deuteronomy 1:17|Deuteronomy 1:17}}; {{2 Chronicles 19:7|2 Chronicles 19:7}}; {{Job 13:10|Job 13:10}}; {{Psalm 82:1-2|Psalms 82:1}}{{Leviticus 19:15-16|–}}{{Psalm 82:1-2|2}}; {{Proverbs 18:5|Proverbs 18:5}}; {{Malachi 2:8-9|Malachi 2:8}}{{Leviticus 19:15-16|–}}{{Malachi 2:8-9|9}}).
Paul's message agreed with the Jerusalem apostles, but their approval did not give Paul his authority ({{Galatians 1:12|1:12}}, {{Galatians 1:16-20|16–20}}).

The apostles in Jerusalem noticed that Paul and Peter focused on different groups in their ministry:

- Peter mainly taught Jewish people ({{Acts 1:1-5:42|Acts 1:1–5:42}}; {{Acts 9:1-10:48|9:1–10:48}}).

- Paul mainly taught non-Jewish people ({{Acts 13:1-28:31|Acts 13:1–28:31}}).

Even though they worked with different groups, they both taught the same good news (gospel) about Jesus.

- *James*: To learn more about James, who was the brother of Jesus. See "James, Brother of Jesus" Profile. 

- *they gave me and Barnabas a right hand of fellowship*: This symbolic handshake showed full acceptance of Paul, Barnabas, their work, and their message.

When Paul talks about helping the poor, this matches the story in {{Acts 11:30|Acts 11:30}}; {{Acts 12:25|12:25}}. The Christians in Judea experienced many years of severe poverty. Paul wanted the non-Jewish churches to help ease this hardship and create unity with the Jewish church (see {{Romans 15:25-27|Romans 15:25–27}}; {{1 Corinthians 16:1-4|1 Corinthians 16:1}}{{Romans 15:25-27|–}}{{1 Corinthians 16:1-4|4}}; {{2 Corinthians 8:1-9:15|2 Corinthians 8:1–9:15}}).

- *When Cephas came to Antioch*: Paul confronting Peter in the city of Antioch is not in the book of Acts, but it likely happened after Paul and Barnabas came back from their first journey to tell people about Jesus ({{Acts 14:26-28|Acts 14:26}}{{Romans 15:25-27|–}}{{Acts 14:26-28|28}}). Paul probably wrote this letter soon after. (The apostle Paul often used the name *Cephas* when writing about Peter in his letters. *Cephas* is an Aramaic word that means "rock" or "stone." In Greek, this same name is *Petros*, which we know in English as "Peter.")

- *he stood condemned*: Peter's actions did not match what he knew—that God accepts non-Jews through faith, not by following the law (see {{Acts 10:1-11:30|Acts 10–11}}). 

- Paul had to confront Peter directly. Paul wanted to protect the good news from being changed ({{Galatians 2:21|Galatians 2:21}}). This meant publicly showing that Peter's public action was wrong (compare {{1 Timothy 5:20|1 Timothy 5:20}}).

Peter knew that Gentiles were accepted into God’s family. Acts chapter 10 tells the story of how God showed that to Peter. But there were Jewish believers who didn’t approve of this. They thought that Jewish believers should stay separate from Gentile believers. They challenged Peter.

Peter started treating Gentiles as outsiders. He no longer treated Gentile believers as his brothers and sisters in God’s family. Other Jewish believers like Barnabas followed his example. They treated Jewish laws as more important than following Jesus together with other believers.

Paul strongly disagreed with Peter. He corrected Peter in public. Then Paul wrote to the Galatians about the law. He was talking about Jewish laws that separated Jews from Gentiles. This included laws about circumcision, food and honouring the Sabbath day. Paul made it very clear that obeying these laws doesn’t make people right with God. Only Jesus can free people from sin’s power and bring them back to God.

Paul described this as if believers are crucified with Christ. This is a picture of how closely believers are joined together with Jesus. Paul wasn’t saying that believers are nailed to the cross. Only Jesus was nailed to the cross and died to save people from sin. Paul was describing something about believers. They no longer live in the sinful ways they used to live in. Those old ways of living are dead. Now believers have new life from Jesus. They don’t receive this new life by obeying the Law of Moses. They receive it from Jesus. It’s a gift because Jesus loves all people.

In Antioch, Peter and others went against their own beliefs and changed the good news about Jesus. This event is not mentioned in the book of Acts. Paul corrected Peter, showing that Paul's role as an apostle was independent of Jerusalem and true to the good news about Jesus.

- Peter ate with the non-Jewish believers because God had shown him it was right ({{Acts 10:9-16|Acts 10:9}}{{Romans 15:25-27|–}}{{Acts 10:9-16|16}}, {{Acts 10:34-35|34}}{{Romans 15:25-27|–}}{{Acts 10:34-35|35}}). 

- James's friends wanted to stop Jewish and non-Jewish believers from eating and meeting together freely. These people insisted that everyone should follow strict Jewish religious customs. They tried to force non-Jewish believers to follow Jewish rules about food and religious practices.

- *he used to eat with the Gentiles. But when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself*: When Peter refused to share meals and the Lord’s Supper (see {{1 Corinthians 11:20-22|1 Corinthians 11:20}}{{Romans 15:25-27|–}}{{1 Corinthians 11:20-22|22}}, {{1 Corinthians 11:33-34|33}}{{Romans 15:25-27|–}}{{1 Corinthians 11:33-34|34}}) with fellow Christians, he created a divide between Jewish and Gentile (non-Jewish) Christians. This suggested that Jewish customs made them more acceptable to God. If not uncorrected, Peter’s actions would have weakened the message of salvation by grace through faith. 

- *for fear of those in the circumcision group*: James's friends pressured Peter so much that he became afraid. This was surprising because earlier, when people criticized Peter for the same thing, he had stood up to them bravely and spoke strong words to defend his actions ({{Acts 11:2-18|Acts 11:2}}{{Romans 15:25-27|–}}{{Acts 11:2-18|18}}). 

Peter might have had two reasons for his actions. First, he might have worried that his actions would make it harder for Jewish people to accept Jesus. Second, he might have been worried about the safety of Jewish Christians in Judea, who were being treated badly by non-Christian Jews (compare {{Galatians 5:11|5:11}}; {{Galatians 6:12|6:12}}). But even if Peter had good reasons, what he did was still wrong.

When Peter acted like a hypocrite, he led other Jewish believers to make the same mistake. They started acting as if people needed to follow Jewish customs to be accepted by God, which went against the good news about Jesus.

- By living like a Gentile (eating with non-Jewish people and not following Jewish food laws), Peter showed that God accepts Gentiles equally with Jews through faith in Christ (see {{Acts 10:34-43|Acts 10:34–43}}; {{Acts 11:17-18|11:17–18}}). 

- *how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews? *Both Jews and Gentiles would understand this from Peter’s actions.

- When Peter and the other Jewish believers stopped eating with non-Jewish believers, they were sending the wrong message. Their actions suggested that believing in Jesus was not enough and that people also needed to follow Jewish laws to be truly accepted by God. Paul strongly argues against this. He explained that we are made right with God only through his kindness (grace) when we believe in Jesus ({{Ephesians 2:8-9|Ephesians 2:8–9}}). 

- We cannot tell exactly where Paul's public words to Peter end and his message to the Galatians begins (see study note on Galatians 2:16). When Paul corrected Peter, he was also correcting the Galatians (see {{Galatians 3:1|3:1}}).

Gentiles were considered "sinners" because they did not have the law and could not obey God's commands. Paul used Jewish thinking categories (compare {{Matthew 15:21-28|Matthew 15:21–28}}; {{Matthew 26:45|26:45}}; {{Luke 6:32-34|Luke 6:32}}{{Matthew 15:21-28|–}}{{Luke 6:32-34|34}}; {{Luke 18:9-14|18:9}}{{Matthew 15:21-28|–}}{{Luke 18:9-14|14}}) with strong irony, emphasizing that everyone is sinful ({{Galatians 2:16|Galatians 2:16}}; {{Romans 3:23|Romans 3:23}}).

Both Jews and non-Jews are sinners. The good news requires everyone to admit their sins (see {{Romans 2:1-5|Romans 2:1}}{{Matthew 15:21-28|–}}{{Romans 2:1-5|5}}; {{Romans 3:1-20|3:1}}{{Matthew 15:21-28|–}}{{Romans 3:1-20|20}}) and seek God's grace ({{Romans 3:21-26|Romans 3:21–26}}). Peter later showed he agreed with this message ({{Acts 15:7-11|Acts 15:7}}{{Matthew 15:21-28|–}}{{Acts 15:7-11|11}}).

Some false teachers were spreading false ideas about Paul's good news. They likely argued that if people did not have to follow the Jewish laws, they would just do whatever sinful things they wanted. Jesus would then be seen as leading people into sin ({{Galatians 2:17|2:17}}). Paul explains how this is not true. Those who trust in Jesus receive strength from the Holy Spirit to live holy lives that honor God (see {{Galatians 5:13-26|5:13}}{{Matthew 15:21-28|–}}{{Galatians 5:13-26|26}}).

- *I prove myself to be a lawbreaker*: Abandoning faith and returning to the law places a person under the law's authority, where everyone faces God’s judgment ({{Romans 3:10-12|Romans 3:10–12}}, {{Romans 3:23-24|23–24}}; see {{Hebrews 6:1-8|Hebrews 6:1}}{{Romans 3:10-12|–}}{{Hebrews 6:1-8|8}}). This act is a serious sin against Christ ({{Galatians 5:2-4|Galatians 5:2}}{{Romans 3:10-12|–}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|4}}; compare {{Hebrews 6:4-6|Hebrews 6:4}}{{Romans 3:10-12|–}}{{Hebrews 6:4-6|6}}). See also study note on 2:19. 

- *If I rebuild*: This refers to insisting on following Jewish laws about food and circumcision ({{Galatians 2:11-13|Galatians 2:11}}{{Romans 3:10-12|–}}{{Galatians 2:11-13|13}}). 

- When Jesus died on the cross, he ended the old system of religious laws that separated Jewish and non-Jewish people from each other and from God ({{Ephesians 2:14-16|Ephesians 2:14}}{{Romans 3:10-12|–}}{{Ephesians 2:14-16|16}}). His death created a new way for all people to come to God through faith.

- *For through the law:* Trying to please God by following the law always leads to sin ({{Galatians 5:2-4|5:2–4}}; see {{Romans 7:5|Rom 7:5}}, {{Romans 7:8-11|8}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Romans 7:8-11|11}}). Living by the Spirit leads away from sin ({{Galatians 5:16|Galatians 5:16}}, {{Galatians 5:22-24|22}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Galatians 5:22-24|24}}). 

- *I died to the law*: "Dying to the law" means stopping the attempt to meet all its demands. Those who trust in Christ share in his death ({{Galatians 2:20|2:20}}). They are no longer judged by the law (see {{Romans 6:2|Romans 6:2}}, {{Romans 6:10-11|10}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Romans 6:10-11|11}}; {{Romans 7:2-6|7:2}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Romans 7:2-6|6}}) and do not see the law as a way to be saved. Instead, Christians live for God in a new relationship with him through Christ ({{Galatians 3:23-4:11|Galatians 3:23–4:11}}; see {{Romans 6:10-11|Romans 6:10}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Romans 6:10-11|11}}; {{Romans 14:7-8|14:7}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Romans 14:7-8|8}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:15|2 Corinthians 5:15}}).

- Paul's good news about Jesus (that we do not need to follow Jewish laws to be saved) does not mean people will just do whatever wrong things they want ({{Galatians 2:17|2:17}}). This is because lawlessness (ignoring or disobeying God's commands) is a response of those who are not redeemed. A redeemed Christian has been crucified with Christ. See also {{Colossians 2:11-14|Colossians 2:11}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Colossians 2:11-14|14}}, {{Colossians 2:20-23|20}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Colossians 2:20-23|23}}. A Christian has left behind the old self, which tried to earn merit by following the law (compare {{Romans 7:4-6|Romans 7:4}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Romans 7:4-6|6}}). 

- *I no longer live, but Christ lives in m*e: Christians have experienced Christ’s death and resurrection ({{Romans 6:1-14|Romans 6:1–14}}). They have new hearts (see {{Jeremiah 31:31-34|Jeremiah 31:31}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Jeremiah 31:31-34|34}}; {{Jeremiah 32:38-41|32:38}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Jeremiah 32:38-41|41}}; {{Ezekiel 11:19-20|Ezekiel 11:19}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Ezekiel 11:19-20|20}}; {{Ezekiel 36:24-31|36:24}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Ezekiel 36:24-31|31}}). These new hearts come through the Spirit's power within them (see {{Romans 8:9-11|Romans 8:9}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Romans 8:9-11|11}}; {{Ephesians 3:16-19|Ephesians 3:16}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Ephesians 3:16-19|19}}; {{Colossians 1:27|Colossians 1:27}}; {{Colossians 3:1-17|3:1}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Colossians 3:1-17|17}}). 

- *The life I live in the body*: Christianity does not say the body is evil or that we must leave this world to have fellowship with God. Instead, by trusting in the Son of God, we fulfill God’s purposes for our lives.

- *who loved me and gave Himself up for me:* Christ’s self-giving love makes new life possible ({{Galatians 1:4|Galatians 1:4}}; {{Romans 8:32-39|Romans 8:32}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{Romans 8:32-39|39}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:16-17|2 Thessalonians 2:16}}{{Galatians 5:2-4|–}}{{2 Thessalonians 2:16-17|17}}).

Paul's opponents in Galatia might have argued that his message made God's grace to Israel meaningless because it was connected to the law (see {{Romans 3:1-2|Romans 3:12}}, {{Romans 3:31|31}}). However, it was actually Paul’s opponents who made God's grace meaningless by denying the need for Christ's death.

- *O foolish Galatians!* Their foolishness was both intellectual and spiritual (compare {{Luke 24:25|Luke 24:25}}; see {{1 Samuel 25:1-38|1 Samuel 25:1–38}}). They stopped trusting in Christ and trusted in the law ({{Galatians 1:6|Galatians 1:6}}). 

- The Galatians were misled by the teachers’ persuasive arguments (compare {{Genesis 3:1-7|Genesis 3:1}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Genesis 3:1-7|7}}). It was not actual witchcraft, but convincing words. 

- *Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified*: When Paul told people about Jesus, he clearly explained how Jesus died and why his death was so important for everyone (see {{Romans 10:14-17|Romans 10:14}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Romans 10:14-17|17}}). Paul helped people understand what the death of Jesus means for them.

Paul compares the Galatians' spiritual experience (see {{Galatians 3:1-5|3:1}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Galatians 3:1-5|5}}) with Abraham's ({{Galatians 3:6-9|3:6}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Galatians 3:6-9|9}}). He shows that both were made right with God through faith, not by following the law ({{Ephesians 2:8-9|Ephesians 2:8}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Ephesians 2:8-9|9}}).

Some Jewish believers in Galatia treated Jewish laws as more important than God’s promises. God had promised to bless all nations and people through Abraham. Jesus’ life and work fulfilled this promise.

Yet some Jewish believers taught that Gentile believers had to obey the Law of Moses. They had to obey it to receive the blessing God promised. Paul explained the difference between having faith in God and obeying Jewish laws. Abraham was made right with God because he believed God and had faith in him.

Some Galatians tried to be made right with God by obeying Jewish laws. This meant that they would have to obey the Law of Moses completely. This was something no one could do. Paul described this like being under the curse of the law. Paul was talking about the covenant curses. He was talking about how no one could perfectly obey the law. He was also talking about Jesus’ death on the cross.

Being put to death on a cross was considered a curse. In this way Jesus became a curse. By doing so he set people free to receive God’s blessings. Everyone who has faith in Jesus receives eternal life and the Holy Spirit.

Paul now defends the truth of his message that a right relationship with God comes by faith in Christ alone. He argues against the idea that non-Jewish people must follow the law to be accepted by God.

The Galatians, like all Christians, received the Spirit by faith in Christ, not by obeying the law of Moses (see {{Acts 2:38-39|Acts 2:38}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Acts 2:38-39|39}}; {{Romans 8:9-11|Romans 8:9}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Romans 8:9-11|11}}; {{2 Corinthians 1:22|2 Corinthians 1:22}}; {{Ephesians 1:11-14|Ephesians 1:11}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Ephesians 1:11-14|14}}; compare {{Acts 10:44-48|Acts 10:44}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Acts 10:44-48|48}}; {{Acts 11:15-18|11:15}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Acts 11:15-18|18}}). God accepted the Galatians because they believed the good news about Jesus (compare {{Romans 10:14-17|Romans 10:14}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Romans 10:14-17|17}}). This made their return to the law unreasonable ({{Galatians 3:3-4|Galatians 3:3}}{{1 Samuel 25:1-38|–}}{{Galatians 3:3-4|4}}).

*are you now finishing in the flesh:* Paul used clever word play to make an important point. The Galatians were trying to become perfect by *human effort* by following the law about circumcising the *flesh* of the male foreskin.

*Have you suffered so much for nothing?* This might mean suffering, but the Galatian church's history does not suggest that. Paul likely referred to the spiritual experiences the Galatians had through the Holy Spirit ({{Galatians 3:3|Galatians 3:3}}, {{Galatians 3:5|5}}). Depending on the law of Moses for a right relationship with God makes the Spirit's work seem meaningless.
*work miracles:* See {{1 Corinthians 12:4-11|1 Corinthians 12:4–11}}. The Holy Spirit is with believers and in the church because they have faith in the good news about Jesus.

This quote is from {{Genesis 15:6|Genesis 15:6}}, where God made his covenant (special agreement) with Abraham (see {{Genesis 15:1-21|Genesis 15:1–21}}; {{Genesis 17:1-27|17:1}}{{Genesis 15:1-21|–}}{{Genesis 17:1-27|27}}). This statement is essential to explain God's relationship with people (see {{Habakkuk 2:4|Habakkuk 2:4}}; {{Romans 4:1-8|Romans 4:1}}{{Genesis 15:1-21|–}}{{Romans 4:1-8|8}}, {{Romans 4:17-22|17}}{{Genesis 15:1-21|–}}{{Romans 4:17-22|22}}).
Abraham's story shows that faith has always been the basis for a relationship with God and for receiving God's promises.

Non-Jewish believers in Jesus are truly part of Abraham's family. They become part of Abraham's family not by following the laws of Moses, but by trusting in God just as Abraham did (see {{Romans 4:9-17|Romans 4:9}}{{Genesis 15:1-21|–}}{{Romans 4:9-17|17}}, {{Romans 4:23-25|23}}{{Genesis 15:1-21|–}}{{Romans 4:23-25|25}}; compare {{Matthew 12:48-50|Matthew 12:48}}{{Genesis 15:1-21|–}}{{Matthew 12:48-50|50}}).

*The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith*: By faith, Abraham expected the coming Messiah (see {{John 8:56|John 8:56}}). He received the message that "all the families of the earth will be blessed through you" ({{Genesis 12:3|Genesis 12:3}}; {{Genesis 18:18|18:18}}; {{Genesis 22:18|22:18}}). God would accept all nations through Abraham's descendant, the Messiah (God's chosen one), in the same way God accepted Abraham—by faith.

Paul here quotes {{Deuteronomy 27:26|Deuteronomy 27:26}}. This verse explains the curse Israel would experience if they did not follow all of God's commands in their covenant with him (see {{Deuteronomy 27:9-26|Deuteronomy 27:9–26}}; compare {{Deuteronomy 28:15-68|Deuteronomy 28:15}}{{Deuteronomy 27:9-26|–}}{{Deuteronomy 28:15-68|68}}; {{Deuteronomy 31:26|31:26}}; {{Joshua 1:8|Joshua 1:8}}; {{Malachi 2:2|Malachi 2:2}}; see also {{Genesis 3:14-19|Genesis 3:14}}{{Deuteronomy 27:9-26|–}}{{Genesis 3:14-19|19}}; {{Genesis 4:10-12|4:10}}{{Deuteronomy 27:9-26|–}}{{Genesis 4:10-12|12}}). Sinful humans cannot fully obey God's will (see {{Romans 3:9-20|Romans 3:9}}{{Deuteronomy 27:9-26|–}}{{Romans 3:9-20|20}}).

The Galatians thought they needed to be circumcised to please God. By doing this, they were trying to follow all of God's laws to be accepted by him. Those who seek to be right with God through the law are under a curse. They cannot follow the entire law, so they cannot receive blessings from it.

- Scripture makes it clear, even if the Galatians or false teachers did not understand, that circumcision is not required for non-Jewish believers. 

- *"The righteous will live by faith"*: Paul quotes {{Habakkuk 2:4|Habakkuk 2:4}}, in which the prophet waits in faith for God's promise to come true.

The law itself is not opposed to faith (see {{Galatians 3:19-25|3:19–25}}; {{Romans 7:7-13|Romans 7:7}}{{Galatians 3:19-25|–}}{{Romans 7:7-13|13}}), but trying to be righteous by following the law opposes righteousness by faith in Christ. Paul quotes {{Leviticus 18:5|Leviticus 18:5}} to show that life under the law of Moses requires obedience rather than *belief*. It is impossible to be accepted by God by trying to obey the law of Moses perfectly ({{Galatians 3:10-11|Galatians 3:10}}{{Galatians 3:19-25|–}}{{Galatians 3:10-11|11}}).

- *redeemed us*: Christ freed his people by paying the price for them (see {{Galatians 4:4-5|4:4–5}}; {{1 Peter 1:18-20|1 Peter 1:18}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{1 Peter 1:18-20|20}}). 

- *"Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree"*: Paul quotes {{Deuteronomy 21:23|Deuteronomy 21:23}}, in which criminals who were killed and had their bodies displayed in public were considered to be under God's curse (see study note on Deuteronomy 21:22). When Jesus was nailed to the cross, he took on God's curse that should have fallen on all sinners (compare {{2 Corinthians 5:21|2 Corinthians 5:21}}).
Unlike those who rely on the law (see {{Galatians 3:10-12|3:10}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Galatians 3:10-12|12}}), people who have faith in Christ receive God's life and blessings freely.

Jesus Christ has given the Gentiles (non-Jewish people) the same blessing promised to Abraham, as described in {{Galatians 3:6-13|3:6}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Galatians 3:6-13|13}}. Paul says this blessing is receiving the promised Holy Spirit ({{Galatians 3:2-6|3:2}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Galatians 3:2-6|6}}; see also {{Romans 8:1-17|Romans 8:1}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Romans 8:1-17|17}}, {{Romans 8:23|23}}; {{Ephesians 1:13-14|Ephesians 1:13}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Ephesians 1:13-14|14}}).
When a person dies, their written instructions about who should receive their property (called a will) cannot be changed. These instructions must be followed exactly as they were written.
Jesus, not the law, has fulfilled the promise and agreement (covenant) made with Abraham.

Abraham’s seed was a way of talking about the children who came after Abraham. Paul used this word to describe Jesus. Jesus was the one from Abraham’s family line through whom God’s promises came true.

The law didn’t stop God’s promise to bless all nations through Abraham. That wasn’t the reason God gave Israel the Law of Moses. God gave the law to show the Israelites how he wanted them to live. The law made it clear what things pleased God and what things were sinful. It gave God’s people ways to deal with the problems their sins caused. In this way it was like a teacher or guard that watched over them.

But the law couldn’t stop the power of sin. Jesus did that. Everyone who believes in Jesus and follows him is made right with God. They are God’s children. They are part of his family no matter who they are. Among believers, no person or group is better or more important than any other. Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free people, males and females are all equal. They are all made one in God’s family because they follow Jesus.

The promises to Abraham were mainly received by him and his child (literally *his seed*). This "seed" was the promised Messiah (God's chosen one), who is Abraham's ultimate descendant. The word "seed" can mean one descendant or many (see {{Genesis 12:7|Genesis 12:7}}; {{Genesis 13:15|13:15}}). Although the promise can refer to many descendants (see {{Galatians 3:29|Galatians 3:29}}; {{Genesis 13:15-16|Genesis 13:15}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Genesis 13:15-16|16}}; {{Genesis 15:5-6|15:5}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Genesis 15:5-6|6}}; {{Genesis 17:7-8|17:7}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Genesis 17:7-8|8}}), it specifically points to one descendant, Christ, who fully fulfilled the promise. The heirs of the promise are not Jacob’s physical children but the spiritual children of Christ, by the Spirit through faith.

- Just as human covenants cannot be canceled ({{Galatians 3:15|3:15}}), the terms of God's covenant with Abraham were not changed when God gave Moses the law. 

- *430 years*: See study note on Exodus 12:40.

The *inheritance* cannot come from obeying the law, because that would cancel God’s promise to Abraham (see {{Galatians 4:1-7|4:1}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Galatians 4:1-7|7}}). This promise was accepted by faith before God gave the law to Moses.

- If people do not receive God's inheritance through the law, why was the law given to Moses? It was to show people their sins and make it clear that sinful actions are wrongs done against God. People cannot rely on their own goodness to save them. Instead, they must trust in God (see {{Romans 3:19-20|Romans 3:19}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Romans 3:19-20|20}}; {{Romans 4:15|4:15}}; {{Romans 5:20|5:20}}; {{Romans 7:7-13|7:7}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Romans 7:7-13|13}}). 

- *until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred*: See {{Galatians 3:16|Galatians 3:16}}. While the promise is permanent, the law of Moses was temporary. With Christ’s coming, the law was fulfilled (see {{Matthew 5:17-20|Matthew 5:17}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Matthew 5:17-20|20}}; compare {{Matthew 3:13-15|Matthew 3:13}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Matthew 3:13-15|15}}; {{John 19:30|John 19:30}}). God's acceptance is based entirely on faith in Christ. 

- *through angels*: {{Deuteronomy 33:2|Deuteronomy 33:2}} in the Greek version (the Septuagint) describes the Lord's coming from Sinai “with myriads of holy ones, angels with him at his right hand.” See also {{Psalm 68:17|Psalm 68:17}}; {{Acts 7:38|Acts 7:38}}, {{Acts 7:53|53}}; {{Hebrews 2:2|Hebrews 2:2}}. 

- *By a mediator*: The mediator was Moses (see {{Exodus 20:19|Exodus 20:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:24-27|Deuteronomy 5:24}}{{Galatians 4:4-5|–}}{{Deuteronomy 5:24-27|27}}). As a mediator, Moses spoke to God for the people and spoke to the people for God.
Paul's argument might make those hearing his message think the law of Moses has no purpose. However, Paul emphasizes the law's true purpose in order to correct false teaching about the law.

- The law of Moses was given through angels and a mediator (Moses). The law required agreement between God and the people. The law was conditional, with blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience. In contrast, God gave his promise directly to Abraham without a mediator. It was God's promise alone, and God did not require anything in return.

- *but God is one*: Paul used the basic Jewish creed (see {{Deuteronomy 6:4|Deuteronomy 6:4}}) to persuade non-Jewish Christians not to convert to Judaism.

There is no conflict of purpose between law and promise or between law and faith. The law works with the promise to help people believe in Jesus. The purpose of the law is to show that people are trapped by their sins ({{Galatians 3:19|3:19}}, {{Galatians 3:22|22}}). It is also meant to help people not sin ({{Galatians 3:23-25|3:23–25}}). 

In Galatia, the Judaizers tried to convince non-Jewish Christians that the law could do something it was never meant to do. The law was never meant to give new life and make people right with God. God does these things based on faith in his promise, which was fulfilled in Jesus Christ (see {{Galatians 3:22|3:22}}).

*all things confined by sin*. See {{Romans 3:9|Romans 3:9}}; {{Romans 7:1-13|7:1}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Romans 7:1-13|13}}; {{Romans 11:32|11:32}}. Following the law of Moses cannot save us. Only believing in Jesus Christ can free us from sin.

Because sin had imprisoned us ({{Galatians 3:22|3:22}}), the law of Moses acted as a guard, keeping God's people safe (*held in custody*) until faith in Jesus was revealed. It clearly showed God's requirements and emphasized the need for a Savior. The law also kept sin under control by clearly showing its consequences.
Paul compares two different times: how God's people lived when they were *under the law* before Jesus came, and how they live now that they belong to Christ and follow him.
The law is like a child's guardian. (The Greek word is *paidagōgos*, meaning "tutor.") In Greco-Roman culture, a guardian was a loyal servant who trained and protected the heir until adulthood.

- *Now that faith has come*: Righteousness by faith was always in effect (see {{Galatians 3:6-9|3:6}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Galatians 3:6-9|9}}), but now, through Jesus Christ, the object of that faith and how people can receive it are clear.

- *we are no longer under a guardian*: In Greco-Roman culture, a child who reached adulthood was no longer under a guardian's control and could govern themselves. Similarly, those who mature through faith in Christ are free from the law's guardianship. They follow Christ directly as he guides them through his word and Spirit.

Those who are God's children through faith in Jesus Christ (see also {{Galatians 4:4-7|4:4}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Galatians 4:4-7|7}}; {{John 1:12|John 1:12}}; {{Romans 9:8|Romans 9:8}}) have come of age as heirs to his promises (see {{Galatians 3:24-25|Galatians 3:24}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Galatians 3:24-25|25}}, {{Galatians 3:29|29}}). They have received a part of that inheritance ({{Galatians 3:14|3:14}}; {{Ephesians 1:14|Ephesians 1:14}}). The Galatians acted unwisely by trying to gain access to God through circumcision ({{Galatians 3:1|Galatians 3:1}}). As God's children by faith, they already had the best possible access to him.
Because of Christ, our condition under faith is different from our condition under the law ({{Galatians 3:23-24|3:23}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Galatians 3:23-24|24}}).

- *For all of you who were baptized into Christ*: See {{Romans 6:3-4|Romans 6:3}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Romans 6:3-4|4}}. Baptism symbolizes the death (or end) of an old life and the birth (or beginning) of a new one. In this new life, the law's curse no longer affects us (compare {{Romans 7:1-6|Romans 7:1}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Romans 7:1-6|6}}). 

- *clothed yourselves with Christ*: Christ covers us and gives us a new identity. Compare {{Colossians 3:12|Colossians 3:12}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:8|1 Thessalonians 5:8}}.

- Now, everyone comes to Jesus and receives God's promises in the same way (see {{1 Corinthians 12:12-13|1 Corinthians 12:12}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{1 Corinthians 12:12-13|13}}; {{Ephesians 2:14|Ephesians 2:14}}; {{Colossians 3:11|Colossians 3:11}}). 

- *male nor female:* Refer to {{Genesis 1:27|Genesis 1:27}}. 

- *you are all one*: Believers form one community, the body of Christ (see {{Romans 12:4-5|Romans 12:4}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Romans 12:4-5|5}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:27|1 Corinthians 12:27}}; {{Ephesians 2:15-16|Ephesians 2:15}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Ephesians 2:15-16|16}}, {{Ephesians 2:19-22|19}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|–}}{{Ephesians 2:19-22|22}}). 

- *in Christ Jesus*: See {{Colossians 2:6-3:11|Colossians 2:6–3:11}}.

Jesus is the ideal descendant of Abraham ({{Galatians 3:16|3:16}}). So, those united with Jesus are also Abraham's children and inherit all his promises ({{Galatians 3:27-28|3:27}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Galatians 3:27-28|28}}).

A child who inherits an estate might get a large fortune. However, before reaching adulthood, the child must follow the rules of guardians and trustees until the time the father decides. In the same way, before Jesus came, God's people were under the guidance of the law of Moses (see {{Galatians 3:23-24|3:23}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Galatians 3:23-24|24}}).
Paul argues that the purpose of the law of Moses for God's children was fulfilled when Jesus came, so we are no longer bound by it.

In Paul’s time, neither children nor slaves had authority in the family. Paul used this as an example to help the Galatians understand more about the good news.

He described Jews as slaves in God’s house. The law was like the guard who watched over them. Paul described Gentiles before they became believers as being slaves to false gods.

Jesus was born under the authority of the law. This meant that the Law of Moses was like the guard watching over him. But he is God’s Son and not a slave. Jesus freed everyone who believes in him from the law. This means that the power of the law no longer rules over Jewish believers. And the power of false gods no longer rules over Gentile believers.

Instead of being slaves, believers are adopted as children into God’s family. They can call God Abba just like Jesus does. They will receive the good things their Father has for them.

Yet the Galatians were turning back to the things they were previously slaves to. Paul couldn’t understand why. They had been so sincere when they first believed the good news. Paul longed for them to be fully committed to the truth about Jesus.

- Before Christ came, God's people were like young heirs to a large estate ({{Galatians 4:1-2|4:1}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Galatians 4:1-2|2}}). They would inherit a great fortune (see {{Galatians 4:5|4:5}}), but they were still under their guardian's care ({{Galatians 3:23-25|3:23}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Galatians 3:23-25|25}}). 

- The basic spiritual principles of this world likely refer to the laws that govern the world without Jesus. These principles were fully expressed in the law of Moses ({{Galatians 3:23-24|3:23}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Galatians 3:23-24|24}}; compare {{Galatians 4:5|4:5}}).

- God chose the perfect time in history for Jesus to come (see {{Luke 4:18-19|Luke 4:18}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Luke 4:18-19|19}}; {{Ephesians 4:8-10|Ephesians 4:8}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Ephesians 4:8-10|10}}). 

- Jesus was fully human, born of a woman, and required to follow the law of Moses. Jesus fulfilled the law (see {{Matthew 3:13-15|Matthew 3:13}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Matthew 3:13-15|15}}; {{Matthew 5:17|5:17}}) so that God's children now have freedom and are no longer enslaved by it. 

- *to redeem those:* By fulfilling the law and taking on its curse, Jesus freed us from its demands ({{Galatians 3:13|Galatians 3:13}}; see also {{Romans 3:24|Romans 3:24}}; {{Colossians 1:13-14|Colossians 1:13}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Colossians 1:13-14|14}}). 

- *that we might receive our adoption as sons:* See also {{Romans 8:15-17|Romans 8:15}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Romans 8:15-17|17}}.

- The Holy Spirit works in our hearts to give us confidence that we are God's children (see {{Romans 8:16|Romans 8:16}}; {{Ephesians 1:13-14|Ephesians 1:13}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Ephesians 1:13-14|14}}). 

- Those with the Spirit of God's Son can call God "Father," just like Jesus did ({{Mark 14:36|Mark 14:36}}; compare {{Matthew 6:9|Matthew 6:9}}).

Before they became Christians, the non-Jewish Galatians worshiped false gods. They worshiped natural things like the sun, moon, and seasons (see {{Romans 1:25|Romans 1:25}}). They lived like slaves to these false gods, constantly afraid they would make them angry ({{1 Corinthians 8:5-6|1 Corinthians 8:5}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{1 Corinthians 8:5-6|6}}).
Paul reminds the Galatians of their past pagan beliefs. He argues that following circumcision and the law is like returning to the same kind of slavery they experienced before they knew God.

- *Now that you know God: *Christians have a relationship with God like a child with a parent, not like a slave with a master ({{Galatians 4:5-7|4:5}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Galatians 4:5-7|7}}). 

- *how is it that you are turning back? *Paul was confused that Christians would want to return to their old life of spiritual slavery ({{Galatians 4:19-20|4:19}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Galatians 4:19-20|20}}). 

- *are known by God*: God is the one who saves and has taken the initiative in understanding their souls and forgiving them freely ({{Psalm 139:1-6|Psalm 139:1}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Psalm 139:1-6|6}}, {{Psalm 139:23-24|23}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Psalm 139:23-24|24}}; {{Luke 2:34-35|Luke 2:34}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Luke 2:34-35|35}}; {{Hebrews 4:12|Hebrews 4:12}}). 

- By *turning back to* circumcision (as a way of being accepted by God), the Galatians would be returning to the same useless spiritual principles they knew when they worshiped false gods. Both ways of living required people to work hard to please a demanding master who was never satisfied.

Circumcision was just one way the Galatians tried to follow the law of Moses. They also started celebrating Jewish festivals. They believed this would make them more acceptable to God. To Paul, this showed they misunderstood or rejected the good news of God's grace through Jesus Christ.

*I fear for you*: The Galatians were in danger of turning away from Christ by depending on the law. If they did, Paul's efforts would have been wasted. The good news would not benefit them (compare {{Hebrews 6:4-6|Hebrews 6:4}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{Hebrews 6:4-6|6}}; {{2 Peter 2:20-22|2 Peter 2:20}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{2 Peter 2:20-22|22}}). See {{Acts 13:44-14:24|Acts 13:44–14:24}} for a description of Paul's work for the Christians in that region.

- *become like me*: Paul was a devoted Jew. He stopped trying to earn righteousness and accepted God's free grace in Jesus Christ. Now, Paul asks these Gentiles to follow his example instead of adopting the Jewish practices he left behind. Paul's advice throughout the rest of the letter ({{Galatians 4:12-6:10|4:12–6:10}}) comes from this single command. 

- *You have done me no wrong:* Similarly, the Galatians should not mistreat Paul now but should continue to warmly accept his ministry and message.
After explaining what the Bible teaches, Paul takes a more personal approach. He reminds the Galatians of their close relationship with him.

- *because of an illness*: Paul might have had a long-term health issue, but we do not know what it was (see {{2 Corinthians 12:7|2 Corinthians 12:7}}). Paul's condition was serious and seemed to cause problems or even upset the new church in Galatia. People often saw physical problems as a sign of God's judgment (see {{John 9:1-2|John 9:1}}{{Colossians 2:6-3:11|–}}{{John 9:1-2|2}}; {{Acts 28:4|Acts 28:4}}). The Galatians looked beyond Paul's physical state and accepted him as God's messenger (literally angel; Greek *angelos*). 

- *as if I were Christ Jesus Himsel*f: See {{Luke 10:16|Luke 10:16}}.

- The Galatians were happy and thankful when Paul shared the good news about Jesus with them. 

- *you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me*: Some think this means Paul had eye problems, but he might have used *eyes* as a symbol for something valuable (see {{Deuteronomy 32:10|Deuteronomy 32:10}}; {{Psalm 17:8|Psalm 17:8}}; {{Matthew 18:9|Matthew 18:9}}). The Galatians were thankful for Pual's message of good news. So, the Galatians would have given Paul their most valuable possession.
At first, the Galatians gladly accepted Paul and his message when they became Christians. But now they were unsure about Paul and possibly even rejected him.

- *Those people are zealous for you:* The Greek word here can mean have a positive meaning, like "eagerness," or a negative meaning, like "jealousy" and "envy." 

- *they want to isolate you from us: *The Judaizers (Jewish Christians insisting on following Jewish laws) might have been so eager because they envied the Galatians’ devotion to Paul and instead wanted the Galatians to be devoted to them (compare 2 Corinthians; see also {{Luke 11:46-52|Luke 11:46–52}}). Another possibility is that the Judaizers wanted the Galatians to depend on them as interpreters of the law of Moses.

It was good for the Galatians to continue eagerly embracing Paul and his message, even when he was not there with them. 

Some English Bibles translate like this: *If someone is eager to do good things for you, that’s all right; but let them do it all the time, not just when I’m with you* (New Living Translation). In this case, Paul might be saying that it was okay for others to seek the Galatians' loyalty, but those teachers were not truly trying to help them.

- The Galatians were like Paul's spiritual children (see {{1 Corinthians 4:14-15|1 Corinthians 4:14–15}}; {{Philemon 10|Philemon 1:10}}). Bringing them to Christ was like giving birth to children and experiencing labor pains. It was difficult but rewarding. Now, Paul felt his work was not finished. 

- *until Christ is formed in you:* Paul uses the picture of giving birth to explain something important. If the Galatians continued to trust in Christ as Paul had taught them, Christ's image would grow in them (they would become more and more like Jesus in how they lived and acted). But if they chose to follow the law instead, this new life would die before it could develop. Paul says he must keep working hard, like a midwife who helps with childbirth, to make sure this does not happen.

If Paul had been there in person, he could have understood his listeners better and adjusted his message to fit their spiritual and emotional needs. From a distance, he was not sure if his tone would be effective.

*Do you not understand what the law actually says?:* The Galatians tried to achieve righteousness through the law, but they did not truly understand its meaning (see {{Luke 24:25-27|Luke 24:25–27}}; {{1 Timothy 1:7|1 Timothy 1:7}}).

Next Paul used Hagar and Sarah as an example. He explained the difference between being a slave and being a child in God’s family.

Hagar and her son Ishmael lived as slaves in Abraham’s house. Paul compared them to Jews living as slaves to the Law of Moses. That started when God established the covenant with his people on Mount Sinai. In Paul’s time, most Jews living in Jerusalem still followed the law.

Paul talked about Mount Sinai, Jerusalem, and Hagar to help explain the Mount Sinai covenant. Sarah and her son Isaac lived as free people in Abraham’s house. Paul compared them to believers living as God’s children in the new covenant. They become God’s children through the power of God’s Holy Spirit.

Paul called their home the Jerusalem that is above. This was another name for the New Jerusalem. Talking about that Jerusalem, the Holy Spirit and Sarah helped Paul explain the new covenant.

Paul taught the Galatians that they shouldn’t live as slaves anymore. In the new covenant they no longer need to live under the law’s authority. They were free people and should live through the power of the Holy Spirit.

- Paul now returns to using Scripture to support his argument. He tells the story of two of Abraham's wives, Hagar and Sarah, and their children. He uses this story to show the difference between two types of people: those who are like slaves because they try to follow all the laws, and those who are free because they belong to Christ.

- Paul uses a special way of explaining Bible stories (called allegory) that Jewish teachers used in those days (see study note on 4:24). Paul was trained as a rabbi (see {{Acts 22:3|Acts 22:3}}) and could effectively debate the Judaizers using their own methods.

Ishmael was the son of the *slave woman*, Hagar. She was Sarah's servant (see {{Genesis 16:15|Genesis 16:15}}). Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham, trying to get the heir God promised through human efforts (see {{Genesis 16:1-4|Genesis 16:1}}{{Luke 24:25-27|–}}{{Genesis 16:1-4|4}}). Isaac, Sarah's son, was born to the *free woman* (see {{Genesis 21:2-3|Genesis 21:2}}{{Luke 24:25-27|–}}{{Genesis 21:2-3|3}}). God did something miraculous to help Sarah have this baby. This fulfilled God's promise (see {{Genesis 17:15-21|Genesis 17:15}}{{Luke 24:25-27|–}}{{Genesis 17:15-21|21}}).

- *serve as illustrations* (literally *are being allegorized*): In allegorical writing, every character and event symbolizes a deeper meaning. Allegorical interpretations often ignore the text's historical meaning and create imaginative meanings. Here, however, Paul understood the story in its historical context and saw it as history. But he interpreted the story's characters as symbols of the current situation. Paul's opponents were also using allegorical methods, so Paul countered their flawed allegory with true allegory (see {{1 Corinthians 9:22|1 Corinthians 9:22}}). 

- *two covenants*: The old covenant (God's special agreement with his people) was formed through Moses. The new covenant came through Jesus Christ. 

- *Mount Sinai… This is Hagar*: Just as Hagar was a slave woman symbolizing human effort, Mount Sinai brought slavery to following the law.

Paul connects Abraham's effort to fulfill God's promises with the attempts in Galatia and other places to achieve salvation by following the law ({{Galatians 4:23|4:23}}). Hagar, as a slave woman, represents Israel's bondage under the law. This contrasts with the freedom of those who have faith in Jesus Christ ({{Galatians 4:26-27|4:26–27}}).

- Both Hagar and Mount Sinai were symbols of Jerusalem. They represented Judaism during Paul's time. Judaism continued to trust in the law and in being Abraham's descendants for their status before God (see {{John 8:31-59|John 8:31}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{John 8:31-59|59}}). They rejected Jesus as Messiah and remained bound to the law ({{Galatians 3:23-24|Galatians 3:23}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Galatians 3:23-24|24}}; {{Galatians 4:1-3|4:1}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Galatians 4:1-3|3}}). 

- *Mount Sinai in Arabia*: Traditionally, Mount Sinai is located in the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt. However, some suggest that* in Arabia* means Mount Sinai was in Midian, where Moses once lived (see {{Exodus 3:1|Exodus 3:1}}).

- Hagar represents slavery to human effort based on Mount Sinai ({{Galatians 4:24-25|4:24}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Galatians 4:24-25|25}}). In contrast, Sarah represents freedom in the heavenly Jerusalem, God's ideal city. Abraham’s true children by faith now live under God's rule in Jesus Christ ({{Galatians 3:29|3:29}}). 

- *she is our mother:* Sarah’s son, Isaac, was freely given all of God's promises apart from the law of Moses. Similarly, Jews and Gentiles who live by faith in Jesus are Sarah’s true children. They receive God's promises to Abraham freely apart from the law ({{Galatians 3:26-29|3:26}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Galatians 3:26-29|29}}; {{Galatians 4:4-7|4:4}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Galatians 4:4-7|7}}).

The quoted passage, {{Isaiah 54:1|Isaiah 54:1}}, promised Israel they would thrive after the exile to Babylon. Those who have faith in Jesus Christ are Sarah’s children ({{Galatians 4:26|Galatians 4:26}}). This fulfills the promise that Sarah, who was childless, would have more children than Hagar, the slave woman. To the Judaizers (those who insisted on following Jewish law), people not following the law might seem *desolate* (spiritually barren or unfruitful), but through faith, they become abundantly fruitful as the bride of Christ ({{2 Corinthians 11:2|2 Corinthians 11:2}}; {{Ephesians 5:31-33|Ephesians 5:31}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Ephesians 5:31-33|33}}).

Paul uses the story of Hagar and Sarah in {{Galatians 4:21-27|4:21}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Galatians 4:21-27|27}} to explain the situation in Galatia. Isaac represents those born through God's promise (see {{Galatians 3:8|3:8}}) by the Spirit's power ({{Galatians 3:2-5|3:2}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Galatians 3:2-5|5}}; see also {{Ephesians 1:13-14|Ephesians 1:13}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Ephesians 1:13-14|14}}). These people trust in God for salvation through Christ by faith. Ishmael represents those who think following the law of Moses will make them acceptable to God ({{Galatians 3:10-11|Galatians 3:10}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Galatians 3:10-11|11}}). This idea would have surprised the Judaizers, who believed they were Abraham's true children because they followed the law of Moses.

Isaac was the promised child. During his weaning celebration, Ishmael treated Isaac badly (see {{Genesis 21:9|Genesis 21:9}}). Similarly, in Galatia, people who insisted on following the law were treating badly those who trusted in God's promise, the message of God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ alone (compare {{Acts 13:50-51|Acts 13:50}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Acts 13:50-51|51}}; {{Acts 14:1-7|14:1}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Acts 14:1-7|7}}).

Sarah's demand about Ishmael in {{Genesis 21:10|Genesis 21:10}} becomes a guideline (see {{Genesis 21:12|Genesis 21:12}}) for dealing with the current son of the slave woman (anyone who refuses to abandon slavery to the law). God does not let those who try to be righteous through their own efforts share in his inheritance (see {{Romans 9:30-33|Romans 9:30}}{{Galatians 4:26-27|–}}{{Romans 9:30-33|33}}). Those who come to God through Jesus Christ alone, by faith and not by following the law, are children of the free woman who inherit God's blessings.

- Paul clearly explains his message to the Galatians. He criticizes their unwise behavior and offers a better choice. That choice is freedom. 

- *Christ has set us free*: Christians are free to live by faith in Christ alone (see {{Romans 8:1-39|Romans 8}}). 

- *do not be encumbered once more* (literally *do not take on a yoke*): A yoke is a heavy wooden bar that joins two farm animals together, like oxen, so they can pull heavy loads. In the Jewish tradition, people used the word "yoke" to talk about following religious laws. It was a duty and honor to "take the yoke of the law." God's children in Jesus Christ are not meant to carry this heavy burden (see {{Luke 11:46|Luke 11:46}}; {{Acts 15:10|Acts 15:10}}). Instead, they follow the gentle guidance of Jesus, which brings freedom instead of heavy demands ({{Matthew 11:28-30|Matthew 11:28–30}}).

Paul encouraged the Galatians to accept the freedom Jesus had given them. But that’s not what other teachers told them.

Other teachers told the Gentile believers in Galatia that males had to be circumcised. That went against what the Jewish believers in Jerusalem had decided in Acts chapter 15. Paul called these teachers troublemakers. He was angry at them for teaching things that weren’t true.

Paul explained why their teachings were dangerous. Jesus had already made the Gentile believers right with God. They didn’t need to be circumcised or obey Jewish laws to be right with God. If they tried to do that, they were saying no to God’s grace.

Paul encouraged the Gentile believers to stop worrying about circumcision. He wanted them to pay attention to having faith in Jesus. He wanted them to show their faith by acting in ways that were loving.
Paul reminded the Galatians who it was that was speaking to them. He was the apostle of Jesus Christ who represented the Lord to non-Jewish people and first preached the good news to them.

The Judaizers were a group who believed in following the law of Moses. They taught that following the law would earn God's favor (compare {{Acts 15:1|Acts 15:1}}). However, this approach actually leads to separation from God. True righteousness comes to those who live in Jesus Christ by the power of the Holy Spirit.
People who try to be righteous by obeying the law must obey every one of its rules without exception (see {{Galatians 2:15-16|2:15–16}}; compare {{James 2:10|James 2:10}}).

People who believe circumcision is needed for salvation depend on the law and themselves, not on Jesus Christ. These people are separated from Jesus and are outside of his grace (see {{Romans 5:2|Romans 5:2}}). They are under the law's judgment. They have lost the benefits of God’s grace (see {{Galatians 1:6|Galatians 1:6}}; {{1 Peter 5:12|1 Peter 5:12}}).

- Instead of living by faith in the law, we can live by completely trusting in the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit helps us become more like what God wants us to be. 

- *eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness*: We receive God’s righteousness at our salvation (see {{Romans 5:9-11|Romans 5:9–11}}; {{Romans 10:10|10:10}}). We receive it in an ongoing way as God's Spirit helps us become more like Jesus ({{Romans 8:1-14|Romans 8:1}}{{Romans 5:9-11|–}}{{Romans 8:1-14|14}}). We receive it fully when Jesus returns and raises us to new life (see {{Romans 8:18-30|Romans 8:18}}{{Romans 5:9-11|–}}{{Romans 8:18-30|30}}). God’s power provides righteousness, and he fulfilles his promise ({{Galatians 3:14|Galatians 3:14}}, {{Galatians 3:22|22}}).

Faith in Jesus Christ gives us all of God's favor and grace, so we cannot gain more through our own efforts. We show our faith by loving others (see {{Romans 13:10|Romans 13:10}}; {{Romans 14:17-19|14:17}}{{Romans 5:9-11|–}}{{Romans 14:17-19|19}}; {{2 Corinthians 8:8-13|2 Corinthians 8:8}}{{Romans 5:9-11|–}}{{2 Corinthians 8:8-13|13}}).

Living by faith is like running a race (see {{1 Corinthians 9:24-27|1 Corinthians 9:24–27}}; {{Philippians 3:13-14|Philippians 3:13–14}}; {{2 Timothy 4:7-8|2 Timothy 4:7–8}}). For the Galatians, the law became an obstacle instead of a support in this race (see {{Luke 11:52|Luke 11:52}}).
The Galatians believed following the law would make God happy, but God did not want them to be bound by it. God wanted them to be free.

This verse was a common saying (literally *A little yeast [or leaven] makes the whole loaf rise;* see {{Matthew 13:33|Matthew 13:33}}; {{Matthew 16:6|16:6}}, {{Matthew 16:11-12|11}}{{Romans 5:9-11|–}}{{Matthew 16:11-12|12}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:6-7|1 Corinthians 5:6}}{{Romans 5:9-11|–}}{{1 Corinthians 5:6-7|7}}). Relying a little on the law for God's acceptance can lead to forgetting that Jesus Christ saves by *his* work alone.

*whoever he may be*: Paul might not have known who the false teachers' were, or he might have thought their qualifications did not matter (compare {{Galatians 2:6|2:6}}). 

*troubling you:* The false teaching distorted the good news, so Paul wrote to clarify their understanding.

- *If I am still preaching: *This likely refers to Paul's preaching as an enthusiastic supporter of Judaism before he converted to Christianity ({{Galatians 1:13-14|1:13–14}}; {{Acts 7:58-8:3|Acts 7:58–8:3}}). As a Christian, Paul never preached that non-Jews must be circumcised. 

- *Why am I still being persecuted?* If Paul had been promoting a religion based on laws, the devoted Jews would not have been persecuting him everywhere he went. These leaders were angry because Paul taught that people did not need to follow the law of Moses to be saved. They thought this teaching was deeply offensive (compare {{Romans 9:33|Romans 9:33}}; {{1 Corinthians 1:23|1 Corinthians 1:23}}).

*emasculate themselves* (literally *cut themselves off;* compare {{Philippians 3:2|Philippians 3:2}}): Paul uses strong words to criticize people who demanded circumcision (cutting off the foreskin from the male sex organ). 

- Paul might refer to pagan priests in Galatia who castrated themselves (removed their testicles) for their gods. Insisting on circumcision for Christians is similar. It involved cutting the flesh to please God through physical actions instead of faith in Christ. 

- Relying on circumcision harmed the false teachers' relationship with God, so they might as well harm themselves physically. 

- In the old covenant, emasculated men could not join the congregation ({{Deuteronomy 23:1|Deuteronomy 23:1}}). Similarly, those who depend on circumcision have no place in the new covenant community. Paul likely wished the Judaizers would *cut themselves off* by leaving the community.

Paul explained how the Galatian believers should use their freedom. Being free from the law didn’t mean that the Galatians could do anything they wanted to do. It meant that they were free to obey God and to serve others out of love.

Paul explained that there are two ways to live. One way is to be controlled by sin. This leads people to do evil things that harm others and themselves. These evil ways have no place in the kingdom of God.

The other way to live is to be led by the Holy Spirit. The Spirit leads people to say no to everything that goes against what God wants. The Spirit leads people to follow Jesus’ example. This is seen in the way that people think, speak and act.

Paul had a name for the ways of thinking, speaking and acting like Jesus. He called them the fruit of the Holy Spirit. These ways don’t depend on rules that control people from the outside. They are the result of the Holy Spirit changing a person’s heart.

Paul explains that justification (being in right relationship with God) comes by faith alone. He then asks, "If we do not follow the law, what guides our behavior?" He answers that the Holy Spirit provides righteousness. The Judaizers (Jewish Christians who believed in following traditional Jewish laws) likely warned that Paul's message of freedom could lead believers to moral failure ({{Galatians 5:1|5:1}}). Paul argues that freedom is not an excuse to sin because love guides Christians. We should use our freedom to serve each other with love (see also {{Galatians 2:20|2:20}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:14-15|2 Corinthians 5:14–15}}).

*The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree*: The followers of Jesus fulfill the law by showing love to every neighbor ({{Leviticus 19:18|Leviticus 19:18}}; see {{Matthew 7:12|Matthew 7:12}}; {{Luke 6:27-36|Luke 6:27–36}}; {{Luke 10:25-37|10:25}}{{Luke 6:27-36|–}}{{Luke 10:25-37|37}}; {{John 13:34-35|John 13:34}}{{Luke 6:27-36|–}}{{John 13:34-35|35}}; {{John 15:9-17|15:9}}{{Luke 6:27-36|–}}{{John 15:9-17|17}}; {{Romans 13:8-10|Romans 13:8}}{{Luke 6:27-36|–}}{{Romans 13:8-10|10}}).

The opposite of love is when people hurt and attack each other (see {{Psalm 35:25|Psalm 35:25}}; {{Proverbs 30:14|Proverbs 30:14}}; {{Jeremiah 8:17|Jeremiah 8:17}}). People who lack love are often bitter and fight with one another. They will eventually harm each other. In contrast, love brings life to others (see {{John 3:16|John 3:16}}; {{John 15:12-13|15:12}}{{Luke 6:27-36|–}}{{John 15:12-13|13}}).

A faith without laws will not cause moral ruin. The Holy Spirit guides people, changing their hearts to follow God's will and not sin (see {{Jeremiah 31:33|Jeremiah 31:33}}; {{Hebrews 8:10|Hebrews 8:10}}).

We cannot just choose to follow the law and not sin. There is a struggle between God's Spirit and our sinful nature (see {{Romans 7:14-25|Romans 7:14}}{{Luke 6:27-36|–}}{{Romans 7:14-25|25}}; {{1 Peter 2:11|1 Peter 2:11}}; compare {{Genesis 4:7|Genesis 4:7}}). The solution is not trying harder to follow the law, but living by God's Spirit. When we are resurrected, we will finally be free from sin (see {{Romans 8:18-25|Romans 8:18}}{{Luke 6:27-36|–}}{{Romans 8:18-25|25}}).

People guided by the Holy Spirit follow the Spirit's authority, not the law. They answer to the Spirit of God, not the law. Paul did not intend to justify breaking civil laws (see {{Romans 13:1-7|Romans 13:1}}{{Luke 6:27-36|–}}{{Romans 13:1-7|7}}; {{Titus 3:1|Titus 3:1}}; compare {{1 Peter 2:13-17|1 Peter 2:13}}{{Luke 6:27-36|–}}{{1 Peter 2:13-17|17}}). He was talking about how to achieve spiritual righteousness before God.

- *The acts of the flesh are obvious *(literally* The works of the flesh are*): Emphasizing law-keeping and sinful actions comes from trying to live without God's Spirit. 

- *obvious*: All people have a basic sense of right and wrong (see {{Romans 1:32|Romans 1:32}}; {{Romans 2:14-15|2:14–15}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:1|1 Corinthians 5:1}}). But some people still choose to do wrong anyway ({{Romans 1:18-21|Romans 1:18}}{{Romans 2:14-15|–}}{{Romans 1:18-21|21}}). 

- The list of acts of the flesh starts with sexual immorality. In contrast, the list of Christian virtues starts with love ({{Galatians 5:22|Galatians 5:22}}). Various kinds of sexual misconduct were common (see {{Romans 1:24-27|Romans 1:24}}{{Romans 2:14-15|–}}{{Romans 1:24-27|27}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:1|1 Corinthians 5:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 6:15-18|6:15}}{{Romans 2:14-15|–}}{{1 Corinthians 6:15-18|18}}; {{2 Corinthians 12:21|2 Corinthians 12:21}}; {{2 Peter 3:10|2 Peter 3:10}}, {{2 Peter 3:18|18}}). In ancient pagan religions, people engaged in sexual activities as part of their worship of fertility gods and goddesses (see {{Revelation 2:14|Revelation 2:14}}, {{Revelation 2:20|20}}). 

- When people sin, they become spiritually unclean and cannot have fellowship with God, who is perfectly pure and holy (see {{Matthew 23:27|Matthew 23:27}}; {{Romans 6:19|Romans 6:19}}; {{2 Corinthians 12:21|2 Corinthians 12:21}}; {{Ephesians 5:3|Ephesians 5:3}}; {{Colossians 3:5|Colossians 3:5}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:7|1 Thessalonians 4:7}}).

These two lists compare life controlled by sinful desires ({{Galatians 5:19-21|5:19}}{{Romans 2:14-15|–}}{{Galatians 5:19-21|21}}) with life guided by the Holy Spirit ({{Galatians 5:22-26|5:22}}{{Romans 2:14-15|–}}{{Galatians 5:22-26|26}}). Living by the Spirit means following a higher moral standard than the law can provide.

- *Idolatry* (the worship of false gods) was common in Galatia and often included *sorcery* ("magic arts," see {{Acts 19:19|Acts 19:19}}; compare {{1 Samuel 15:23|1 Samuel 15:23}}; {{Revelation 9:21|Revelation 9:21}}; {{Revelation 18:23|18:23}}; {{Revelation 21:8|21:8}}; {{Revelation 22:15|22:15}}). It also often included sexual immorality (compare {{1 Corinthians 6:9|1 Corinthians 6:9}}, {{1 Corinthians 6:15-20|15}}{{Romans 2:14-15|–}}{{1 Corinthians 6:15-20|20}}). 

- *Hatred* causes people to fight with others, which is the opposite of the Holy Spirit's way of humility and love ({{Galatians 5:22-23|Galatians 5:22}}{{Romans 2:14-15|–}}{{Galatians 5:22-23|23}}). 

- *Discord* means causing arguments and looking for fights, not peacefully defending what is right ({{1 Corinthians 3:3|1 Corinthians 3:3}}; {{2 Corinthians 12:20|2 Corinthians 12:20}}; {{1 Timothy 6:4|1 Timothy 6:4}}; {{Titus 3:9|Titus 3:9}}).
